descriptions.value: José Viñals officiated and recorded the May 24th, 1801 burial of Mursyte (Spanish name Cecilio Jose or Cecilio Joseph Mursyte), age 40 of “rancheria de Excelen,” writing that Mursyte had died “en el monte” from having been “despedazado del oso.” Viñals’s specific reference to ‘the mountain’ is significant to this history. Though alone, this singular tense reference to the site of the 1801 encounter between Mursyte and the Bear would does not allow for the responsible identification of a particular site in relationship to this microhistory, a hypothesis can be formed based on its emergence elsewhere in the record in view of the common qualities between particular historical narratives. This is the second appearance of this phrase in connection to fatal or highly injurous Bear encounters among Indigenous individuals. Their stories become visible in the data at the same time of year and among individuals whose histories describe common ancestral land relationships which the record reveals as specific to the same place or origin. Juan Amorós‘s 1806 reference to “el monte” near Excelen as the site of encounter between Alayua (a previously-unbaptized Indigenous man, baptism number 02602) and a Bear mirror exactly the language with which Viñals refers to the site of Mursyte’s fatal 1801 encounter (see T.GB.1806.1). This connection is not purely causal, but is made significant by indicative social and seasonal facets. Of the latter, it is compelling to note that the 1801 encounter takes place on May 23rd, that of 1806, on or in the days immediately prior to May 27th. Again where this could be dismissed as incidental, it is worth considering the mutual ancestral land relationships which mission records describe of the involved Indigenous individuals and communities. As is the case for T.GB.1806.1, mission records describe familial and ancestral relationships to the Esselen community of “Excelen:” in Mursyte’s baptismal record of July 1777, Junipero Serra describes Excelen as both Mursyte’s origin and that of both his father, Yampas, and his mother, Tzueles. This land relationship is also consistent for the spouse described in Mursyte’s burial record: marriage record of Mursyte and Genovefa Maria (Spanish name, baptism number 00791) also describes her ancestral connection to Excelen and Eslenaj (marriage number 00211). Her baptismal record of 1783 deepens these connections, wherein Serra’s notes decribe this ancestral land relationship along a matrilineal line. The convergence of these factors is not prescriptive, but suggests a potential relationship between community, seasonal activities, geography, and, potentially, location. By this basis, a representative location has been set based on this history. That Mursyte‘s burial data denotes a spousal relationship with Genovefa Maria in turn implicates the life of her daughter, Matrona Maria (Spanish name, baptism number 00787, father, to whom Serra refers as “Xéchu,” also of Excelen) in association with this history. T.GB.1801.1, Early California Population Project Database, Baptism number 00461, Burial number(s): 01370. Content notice: engage this history with respect and care. descriptions.value: Juan Amorós recorded the October 10th, 1819 provisional baptism of Sunipamele / Lotés (Spanish name, Francisco de Borja), describing the 25 year old as being in ‘imminent and evident‘ danger of dying after being gravely injured by a bear (“el qual se hallava con proximo y evidente peligro de morir por causa de haverlo herido gravemente un oso“). A suppli ceremonia date to follow this baptism on the 28th of July, 1821, and and a burial record from 1833 associated with mission San Francisco Solano (number 00556) confirm that Sunipamele survived his encounter with the Bear. As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). Amorós describes the location of the baptism as “Tulme rancheria,” “en el ultimo de los esteros de la nacion de los Petaluma” describes the location of Tulme, Susúli, and Tuchayelin in the wetlands on the upper reaches of the Petaluma River. Sunipamele‘s condition as noted by Amorós strongly suggests that the encounter occurred within reasonable proximity to this community. A representative location has been set based on this history. Sunipamele‘s baptismal record describes the incorrect baptism numbers for his father and mother. His father is Euele or Ebele (Spanish name, Pacomio, baptism number 00571), his mother, Llamutac or Lumutaca (Spanish name, Pacomia, baptism number 00572). Sunipamele had a brother, Taxco (Spanish name Asisclo or Acisclo, baptism number 00058), baptized at Capilla in 1818, and records refer to a sibling of both, described by the names Valentin or Valentina across records, of stated origin San Francisco. The family‘s baptismal records also describe Sunipamele‘s (paternal) uncle, Utiac (Spanish name, Pelagio, baptism number 00569), and aunt, Hohosél or Ouhooc (Spanish name, Pelagia, baptism number 00330). It is possible that these two were the parents of Valentina, though further record at present appears limited. Sunipamele‘s burial data does not describe a spousal relationship associated with San Rafael Arcángel. T.GB.1819.1, Early California Population Project Database, Baptism number 00325, Burial number(s): 00556. Content notice: engage this history with respect and care. descriptions.value: Juan Amorós officianted and recorded the May 27th, 1806 provisional baptism of Alayua (Spanish name, Juan de Dios), age 40, by Ignacio Ortega. Amorós‘s entry notes that Ortega performed the rite on “el monte,“ following Alayua “having been bitten by a bear on the mountain“ (“haviendo mordido un oso en el monte“). A suppli ceremonia date to follow this baptism on June 8th, 1806 and a burial record from 1823 (number 02462) confirm that Alayua survived his encounter with the Bear. As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). Amorós describes Ignacio as “mayordomo” of mission San Carlos Borromeo (“mayordomo de esta mision”). In order to avoid the possibility of confusion it is necessary to mention that an Indigenous boy associated with mission San Carlos Borromeo at this time also appears in mission records under this name, but is not the Ignacio involved in this particular history. The Ignacio Ortega to whom Amorós refers as “mayordomo de esta mision” is the son of Capt. Jose Francisco Ortega. He appears in both record of Ortega‘s provisional baptism of Alayua in 1806 and the baptism of a then-four-year-old Indigenous boy assigned the name of the man appointed his Godfather, this son of Capt. Ortega, in 1805. The boy was baptized by Amorós at age four, of stated origin “Sancones” (described by the ECPP as Ensen), the son of Coyote Siqueis (baptism number 02671, described as “capitan de Sancones”) and Putxaxtams (baptism number 02672)), with AMR of the ECPP noting of the boy‘s baptismal record in July of 2003 that Amorós included the explanation that this was the name he received at baptism (“llamado de gentil Ignacio Ortega: cuyo nombre se quedo en el bautismo”). Though Amorós‘s specific reference to ‘the mountain‘ and Ortega‘s decision to administer the provisional baptism on site suggests the dire nature of Alayua‘s injuries and lends itself to the possibility that the location of baptism may likely describes the site of encounter between Alayua and the Bear (or one quite local to it), Amorós‘s reference to the mountain using the singular tense does not alone allow for the identification of a particular site in relationship to this microhistory, and should be interpreted cautiously. Alayua‘s baptism record describes a spousal relationship with Jauna (Spanish name, Maria Monserrate, born c.1773-1832, baptism number 02599), with whom it is described he shared one daughter within the mission system, Jacinta (Spanish name, 1805-1820, baptism number 02513). Their familial relationships can be corroborated across the burial and baptism records of these family members. Baptismal record describes Alayua‘s origin as “Excelen,“ a land relationship also consistent for Jauna and Jacinta. A representative location has been set for this microhistory local to the geography of Excelen. descriptions.value: Juan Cortés recorded the April 4th, 1805 provisional baptism of Lionahuit (Spanish name, Martin), age 64, at “rancheria de Siguaya“ by Malasuit (Spanish name, Venancio or Venancio Joseph, baptism number 00301, also referred to as Amalachuit (see T.GB.1804.1)), writing that Lionahuit had been ‘gravely injured by a Bear‘ (“gravemente herido por un oso”). Both Lionahuit‘s burial on April 6th, 1805 (burial number 01223) and the lack of a subsequent “suppli ceremnonia” describe the fatality outcome of this event. As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). Amalachuit‘s identity is confirmed through spousal relationship to Silmaioguo (Spanish name, Maria Ana or Mariana), c.1785-1811 (see: T.GB.1804.1). The record of Lionahuit‘s provisional baptism describes familial relationships to two individuals within the mission Santa Barbara system of unstated type: Puialaut, or Puialauta (Spanish name, Simon or Simon Joseph, c.1771-1825, baptism number 00607), and Martiniana (Spanish name, c.1772-1805, baptism number 01472) with whom Puialaut is listed as being in a spousal relationship (as described by marriage number 00394). The exact nature of the familial relationship between these two individuals and Lionahuit is not explicitly referenced. A representative location has been set based on this history. descriptions.value: Estevan Tápis recorded the August 19th, 1804 provisional baptism of Salunihuiaut (Spanish name, Sebastian), age 64, by Amalachuit (Spanish name, Venancio, baptism number 00301, also referred to as Malasuit (see T.GB.1805.1)) at “rancheria de Tequeps,“ writing that Salunihuiaut was ‘seriously injured as a result of having been attacked by a bear‘ (“gravemente lastimado de resultas de haber sido acometido de un oso”). Neither burial record nor a subsequent “suppli ceremnonia” date describe the fatality outcome of this event. As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). The fatality outcome of this event describes an unknown outcome, but acknowledges that the possibility of fatality is feasible. Salunihuiaut‘s provisional baptism record describes no familial relationships within the Santa Barbara mission system. This record will be updated if additional information further contextualizes this microhistory becomes available. Of additional note, that Tápis describes Amalachuit‘s occupation as an “Ynterprete” is in this respect significant. The location to which this record refers (“Tequeps”) is a Chumash village and community site where additional provisional baptisms, also provided in response to severe injury following Bear encounter, also described by Tápis, and for which interpreters acting on behalf of the mission to perform provisional baptisms are known to have occurred (see entry T.GB.1799.2). In this regard, Amalachuit‘s role as officiant of this provisional baptism describes both baptismal trend and important ancestral relationships between Chumash communities, bears, and place in which mission relationships became entangled. The baptismal record of Amalachuit‘s daughter Rita (Spanish name, baptism number 03004, c.1804-1804) describes his origin as “rancheria de Alcajch.” Baptismal record for his mother, Fermina (Spanish name, born c. 1736-1817, baptism number 00897), in 1796, also denotes her origin as “rancheria de Alcajch,” describing familial bonds to a distinct location from Tequeps, where the provisional baptism of August 1804 was administered by Amalachuit many years later. Though this in itself is certainly not unusual, Amalachuit‘s marriage to Silmaioguo (Spanish name Maria Ana, or Mariana, c.1785-1811, baptism number 01486) describes her family connection to Tequeps, giving cause to consider Amalachuit‘s personal connection to, and role in, this community. Baptismal record for Silmaioguo‘s mother, Sicsapehue (Spanish name, Ygnacia Maria, born c. c.1774-1808, baptism number 02957) also describes “Tequeps” as her origin, deepening ancestral connection to this site along matrilineal lines. A representative location has been set based on this history. T.GB.1804.1, Early California Population Project Database, Baptism number 03039, Burial number(s): Unknown. descriptions.value: Juan Cortés recorded the provisional baptism of Telemoguiauta (Spanish name, Ysidoro), age 59, on January 2nd, 1803 at “Calahuasa [rancheria],“ with Cortés writing that the rite was performed due to danger of imminent death following an encounter with a Bear (“por hallarse de peligro a causa de haverlo mordido un oso”). Across both baptismal and burial record, Cortés describes Telemoguiauta as “capitan de dicha rancheria.”  As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). The provisional baptism was performed by Jose Ortega (who Cortés describes as (“sargento ynvalido”), likely, José Maria Ortega (1760-1822), son of José Francisco Ortega (1734-1798)). Burial record describes an alternate spelling of Telemoguiauta‘s Native name (Telemoguisauta), and neither spousal nor parental relationships are described. Though neither the exact date of burial nor death are described by this record, Cortés‘s notes in the March 21st, 1803 entry determine the fatality relationship of this event. Per AMR‘s April 2004 note, Cortés wrote of Telemoguiauta‘s burial: “I certify having learned with certainty that he died at the rancheria of Calahuasa… his body was buried at said rancheria” (“Certifico haver sabido con certeza haver muerto en la rancheria de Calahuasa… su cuerpo fue sepultado en [dicha] rancheria”). A representative location has been set based on this history (the Santa Ynez Indian Reservation is the site of Calahuasa Ranchería). descriptions.value: Juan Cortés officiated and recorded the June 26th, 1798 provisional baptism of Bosie (Spanish name, Benbenuto) at Pasheeknga (to which Cortés refers as “Passenga“), a major Tongva village northwest of Achooykomenga (the Tongva village in which the mission was established), writing that a seventy-year-old man was in a state of extreme need having sustained serious injuries from an encounter with a Bear (“en extrema necesidad... que havia maltratado bastante un oso”). Bosie was buried four days later on June 30th, 1798, at the mission‘s church. As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). Cortés refers to Passenga as a site not far from the mission San Fernando Rey de España (“sitio llamado Passenga poco distante de esta Mision“), aligning with the geography of Pasheeknga and Achooykomenga, populous Tongva villages. It may be that the encounter between Bosie and the Bear occurred near this area, and a representative location has been selected to represent this geography because the primary source does not support the inference that movement between the site of Bosie‘s origin (Momonga) and the location at which he was provisionally baptized by Cortés (at Pasheeknga) occurred, or is likely. Yet that Cortés describes Bosie‘s origin as “Rancheria de Momonga“ may complicate this reading and further contextualize recent readings of its social history. Momonga acted as a significant cultural, spiritual, artistic, and settlement site and may have been associated with individuals of elevated social status. To this, Knight (2018) counters John Romani‘s 1981 assertion that Momonga was a “highly prestigious village occupied by high status individuals” rather than “a village of commoners or a more secular assortment of individuals”, postulating instead that Momonga may more accurately represent “actually (only) the ceremonial area for an extended village” ((See: Knight, Rock Art at Momonga (CA-LAN-357), 1, 3-4)). Knight further argues that the expanse of Momonga‘s influence “may have included all (or most) of the many sites found from the L.A./Ventura County line on the west,” serving geographies “as far east as CA-LAN-21 [the Walker’s Chatsworth Carin Site] and CA-LAN-209,” both of which he describes as near the mouth “of Brown’s Canyon, to the east” (near Canoga Avenue) (Knight, Rock Art at Momonga (CA-LAN-357), 3-4). Further, in-field observations made by Edwin Krupp and Albert Knight in 2016 identified seasonal aspects to the sacred geography of Momonga which may further contextualize this history (Knight, Rock Art at Momonga (CA-LAN-357), 6). Their observations found that, observed from the south edge of its peak upon the winter solstice, sunset projects the shadow of Stoney Point on the “main panel outcrop” of CA-LAN-357, acting as a sundial (Knight, Rock Art at Momonga (CA-LAN-357), 6). This finding describes the seasonal land relationships which dictated the placement of sacred artwork sites in the Simi Hills: “the earth itself indicates which outcrop has the proper significance to qualify as the most sacred place in the area” for the placement of sacred art (Knight, Rock Art at Momonga (CA-LAN-357), 6). Such information may assist in contextualizing further seasonal or social land relationships which may prove relevant to the encounter between Bosie and the Bear in June of 1798, and, more broadly, supports a reading of dialogue between Momonga and more easterly sites in the San Fernando Valley like Passenga, Achooykomenga and the related, pre-mission Pueblo de Los Ángeles, established in 1781. A representative location has been set based on Cortés‘s description, the approximate location of several significant cultural sites specific to Momonga as described in Knight (2012) as a baseline (Knight, “Three Chumash-Style Pictograph Sites in Fernandeño Territory,” 2). Dialogue between Momonga and Tochonanga, a Tataviam village on the Santa Clara River, may prove relevant to this history. descriptions.value: Estevan Tapis recorded the private provisional baptism of Chuluascucáy (Spanish name, Francisco de Jesus), an eight year old boy of “rancheria de Najalayegua,“ officiated by Junait (Spanish name Urbano or Urbano Joseph, c.1775-1794) on June 8th, 1794 at “rancheria de Chniguaj,“ writing that the child had been ‘gravely bitten‘ by a Bear (“mordido gravemente de un osso”). It would seem that Chuluascucáy survived the Bear encounter, as a “suppli ceremonia” date of January 18th, 1795 officiated by Estevan Tapis is recorded, and “Francisco” is referred to in his father’s baptismal record (as well as a brother, “Maxin” (referred to as “Magin” in their mother‘s baptismal record that same year), baptism number 00827) on March 26th, 1796. As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). The presence of Junait in association with Estevan Tapis and “rancheria de Chniguaj,” elsewhere implied to be difficult to access may suggest a continuation of Tapis‘s pattern of deploying boys baptized early in the mission‘s history to act as interpreters for Mission Santa Barbara (refer to T.GB.1798.2, for example). Junait was baptized in 1787 at mission Santa Barbara (baptism number 00056, then age 12). Chuluascucáy‘s baptismal record refers to Junait‘s spousal relationship with Aloria (Spanish name, Serafina or Seraphina Maria baptism number 00103)), an Indigenous girl of “rancheria [...] Saxpilil,” or “Xaspili,” also baptized in 1787 at age eleven. Marriage number 00053, officiated by Christoval Oramas on the 18th of February, 1788 (when Aloria was twelve and Junait was thirteen), corroborates their identities via baptismal numbers and place relationships (and provides a potential, additional disambiguation for “Siutu,” Junait‘s origin, here referred to as “Siugchi”). Junait was not buried until December of 1794 (burial number 00261), further corroborating his identity in relation to this role. That Junait officiated this provisional baptism for a severe injury related to Bear encounter in 1794 contributes to understanding another provisional baptism that follows in 1798 and which describes similar circumstances. Also officiated by an Indigenous man baptized early in the mission‘s history (Najaita, Spanish name Luis or Luiz), the c. June 20th, 1798 encounter between Francisca (Spanish name), a seventy-year-old woman from Chniguaj, and a Bear contributes alongside this history towards both further identifying the tightly-linked geography of these histories and localizing the seasonality of Bear encounter. A comparative review of the locations relevant to these events is addressed by ______, which describes several realted or potentially-related etymological disambiguations which may strongly suggest that these events occurred within a highly specific geography. Social context may further develop geographic understanding established by this previous entry. This entry will be updated should additional information relating to the relationship between the geographic settlement area or community sites represented by these histories become available. The occurrence of these events at the same time of year is particularly significant. A representative location has been set based on this history in relation to that of T.GB.1798.2 pending further information. Marriage number 00421 of May 29th, 1802 refers to Chuluascucáy and Romualda Maria (c.1786-?, baptism number 00466, her origin denoted as Geló), corroborates his baptismal number, parents and their associated baptismal data, and refers to his origin by the disambiguation “Snajalayegua,” after which point, Chuluascucáy vanishes from the record. A subsequent marriage record for Romualda Maria may describe this as more than a factor of the fragmented nature of these archives or otherwise distinguish this history from mere archival anomaly. Record for Romualda Maria‘s marriage to Yayamehuit (Spanish name, Raimundo, of Estuco, baptism number 02635) on January 17th, 1808 (marriage number 00854), refers to Chuluascucáy as a former spouse, but does not describe a date for his burial record or its associated number (the ECPP denoting “?” in the latter field). descriptions.value: Jose de Miguel recorded the June 20th, 1798 provisional baptism of “Francisca” (Spanish name) took place at “rancheria llamada Sinojoso,“ owing, the record describes, to her being ‘at the point of death’ following an encounter with a Bear (“in articulo mortis... a quien mordio el oso“). The provisional baptism was officiated by Najaita (Spanish name, Luis or Luiz), an Indigenous man fourth baptized in association with mission Santa Barbara (at the age of ten), acting as an interpreter for Mission Santa Barbara. The ECPP refers to the officiant of this baptism as “Luis, de Miguel, Jose” in Franisca‘s baptismal record: this is an amalgamation of Jose de Miguel and Najaita‘s Spanish name. The baptismal record records Francisca as 70 years of age at the time, suggesting a birth year of approximately 1728. Francisca survived the Bear encounter, and a burial record describes her passing in February of 1819. Importantly, no date is recorded for the “suppli ceremonia.” As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). Reference to “Sinojoso” in this record (elsewhere referenced as Senojoso) is of potential use in contextualizing to the geography of this history. Though the location of the Chumash village to which this hispanicization refers is relevant to, and may be local to, the encounter between Francisca and the Bear, and though its relevance to the missionary project of the mission Santa Barbara is known, its location is simultaneously not well understood or documented in colonial archives and very important to identify for the purposes of the human-animal relationships this dataset seeks to evidence: on June 26th, 1798, an additional baptismal record suggests another, or perhaps related, instance of human-Bear conflict which occurs four years prior at the same month (season) in what appears to be the same site, or within this same area (see Engelhardt, 1923, 448-449, see baptism number 00789 and T.GB.1794.1 for further details). Engelhardt 1923 references a potential relationship with place names including “Chisolop,  Sisolop Chnajalayegua  lChniguaj,  Sniguaj Choloosos (on  island) Chuccu,  Succu  (Rin-con).” A comparative review of ECPP data further contextualizes the disambiguation “Sniguaj” in ways productive towards identifying the geography of this history, and so, the site of Francisca‘s encounter with the Bear. Francisca‘s baptismal record refers to her relative, Muemeyaxu, who holds one of the earliest baptism numbers associated with mission Santa Barbara (Baptism number 00006). Muemeyaxu (referred to variously across several records by multiple hispanicizations of his Native name Memeyaxu, Mamayaso, and Muemeyaxu, and by disambiguations of his Spanish name, “Juan Joseph,” including “Juan Jose,” and “Juan Josef”) was baptized January 24th, 1787 at the age of 18 by Antonio Paterna (implying a year of birth c.1769). At the time of Muemeyaxu‘s baptism at “la que servia de Yglesia” (this note of Paterna‘s adding material context to the early nature of this rite), his origin is referred to as the “rancheria llamada Snigua,” and while neither his father nor mother are referred to by name, the baptismal number 01402 is associated with his father. This baptismal record (also a provisional rite), administered on January 16th, 1800, identifies Muemeyaxu‘s father as “Francisco Maria,” identifying his paternal relationship with Muemeyaxu by both his Spanish name (“Juan Josef”) and baptismal number, and corroborating both the elder man‘s age (60 years old at time of baptism, born c.1740), and both his origin and the place at which the rite was performed as “Sniguaj,” or “rancheria de Sniguaj,” respectively. Francisco Maria‘s baptismal record also refers to a spousal relationship between Maria Guadalupe and his son Muemeyaxu, correlating with what is recorded in Francisca Maria‘s baptismal record. A search of baptismal records associated with “Sniguaj” as the place of baptism yields some additional insight into the geography of this location. A series of four baptisms conducted on the 8th of May, 1801 reveal a particular gender dynamic associated with this location: all are Native women, all experienced provisional baptisims, all are over the age of seventy, and across several, Juan Cortés‘s line explaining that “todos imposibilitados por su ancianidad y achaques de venir a la Mision” (all unable to come to the Mission due to old age and infirmities) is applied. This may (to say nothing of hesitation on more social grounds), suggest either difficulty or length of the journey between these locations (that Engelhardt associates this term with island Chumash communities is worth noting within this context, but data is not yet explicitly supportive of this). However, further supporting the distance suggested by Cortés is the emergence of another trend. In particular, the consistent utility and presence of baptized, Indigenous interpreters by Estevan Tapis - specifically, Najaita (corroborated as a consistent figure by reference to his wife, Justa Maria, throughout these records) - may suggest social and geographic factors which account for the difficulty to which Cortés later alludes, and the spatial relationship between mission Santa Barbara and this mission (Najaita acted at officiant for baptism numbers 00747 in 1793 and 01287 in 1798, both of which provisional). Importantly, these histories reveal further disambiguations which corroborate the relationship described by Engelhardt, broadening archival scope: in particular, “rancheria de Chniguaj” appears in these baptismal records (see, for example, provisional baptisms 01508 of September 5th, 1800, and 01522 of November 5th 1800, both officiated by Vicente Maria, Indigenous interpreter and recorded by Estevan Tapis). The baptismal record for “Francisca” do not identify whether Guisulato, her spouse‘s stated name at that time, and “Francisco Maria” (the Spanish name he was assigned after his own provisional baptism two years after her own) are the same person, nor confirm or deny her parental relationship to Muemeyaxu, the histories of both elders are united in shared community, place relationship, and familial ties to both Muemeyaxu and Maria Guadalupe (the spouse to which his baptismal and burial records refer). Further, that Najaita officiates provisional baptisms across two of the most prevalent place name disambiguations which appear to, or may, relate to the same geographic settlement area or community, including that associated with Francisca, adds credence to the possibility that these sites may relate to or represent the same geography and is thus worthy of note. It may be of use to consider the gendered roles of elderly women in the transmission of Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) in Chumash society, with specific attention to the role of female elders in summer berry harvesting and burn practices, both of which occur in lowland areas into which brown bears moved during the spring summer transition to access the same energy flows (see: Tasoff, “A Chumash Cultural Burn Reignites Ancient Practice for Wildland Conservation,” Santa Barbara Museum of Natural History, 2023). In the event that this information in future proves to be correlated with this history, that burning practices were outlawed by the Spanish in May of 1793 (just five years prior to Francisca's encounter with the Bear) may offer further context. The coorelation between several of the sites, and their potential correlation to Engelhardt_s reference to correlation between Chalajuaj and Montecito aligns with this potential geography. For lack of additional context on the location of this village, a representative location near mission Santa Barbara has been set based on this history. Francisca‘s baptismal record describes a spousal relationship with “Guisulato.” “Juan Jose” (Spanish name), for whom the baptismal record suggests a spousal relationship with “Guadalupe” (Spanish name), are also identified as Francisca‘s relatives at the time of her provisional baptism. The record of Francisca‘s 20th February, 1819 burial record corroborate Juan Jose as her relative and denote his Native name as Memeyaxu. descriptions.value: Buenaventura Sitjar officiated and recorded the June 20, 1795 provisional baptism of Tamác (Spanish name, Antonio), conducted in the presence of Tamác‘s father, Achètas (Baptism number 03269X). Tamác, ‘having been bitten by a bear‘ (“por averlo mordido un oso”), was not expected to survive. His provisional baptism was performed near mission San Antonio de Padua “[en su rancheria], Quinau.“ Tamác survived his June 1795 encounter with the Bear, with Sitjar recording that the “Supli Ceremonia” was performed on August 30th, 1795, at which time Tamác was taken to mission San Antonio de Padua (“lo lleve á la Ygl.a y le supli todas las ceremonias”). Historical precedent strongly suggests that Tamác was resettled to San Antonio de Padua at this time. As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). While further details on the specific location of the Bear encounter are not available, the locality of Quinau positions the likely landscape of encounter within the vicinity of this known Salinan settlement area, describes proximity to the mission itself, the San Antonio River, and the Santa Lucia Mountains (See: Milliken and Johnson, An Ethnogeography of Salinan and Northern Chumash Communities – 1769 to 1810, 2005, 10, 52, 143-144). A representative location has been set based on this history. Tamác‘s burial date reflects longterm survivability of the Bear encounter. descriptions.value: Fermin Francisco de Lasuen officiated and recorded the July 27, 1786 provisional baptism of Ponohi (Spanish name, Pantaleon Maria), “whom a Bear had seriously wounded” (“a quien hirio gravemente un oso”) “due to the danger of death” (“propter periculum mortis”). The Baptism was performed at “Ensen entre los parages de Buenavista y...Zanjones“ near mission San Carlos Borromeo, with José Señan officiating the Supli Ceremonia, performed almost exactly four years later on July 12th, 1790. As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). The delay between Ponohi‘s provisional and “suppli ceremonia” baptism should be noted for this reason. Owing to a lack of further detail, the representative date assigned to this history reflects its latest possible occurrence (the date of baptism). Both Ponohi‘s previously-unbaptized status and recorded origin of “Ensen” should prompt consideration of this history's relationship to ancestral, seasonal energetic streams and the associated, genered labour roles of Rumsen Ohlone communities as relevant to historical Kinship practices and human-Bear encounter in the Salinas Valley and associated foothills. The location to which Fermin Francisco de Lasuen refers between “Buenavista” and “Zanjones” describes an area of ancestral significance for Rumsen Ohlone communities communities (See: Culleton, James, Indians and Pioneers of Old Monterey, 1950, 177, 236). While the precise date of encounter between Ponohi and the Bear is unknown, and the geography described as his point of origin (or at least, potentially, his locality at the time of baptism or Bear encounter) is neither causal nor definitive, Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) of Rumsen Ohlone summer hunting practices provides important context. The gendered lines along which hunting labour fell are also significant. A representative location has been set based on this history. Ponohi (Pantaleon Maria)‘s burial data denotes no spousal or familial relationships associated with San Carlos Borromeo. His baptismal and burial records suggest that he was born c.1760-d.1825. descriptions.value: Antonio Cruzado recorded the October 25, 1777 baptism of “Maria Liberata” (Spanish name) at San Gabriel Arcángel, writing that a provisional baptism was performed “en caso de necessidad...mordida de un oso.” As the ECPP Guide for Users explains, “the padres also baptized individuals who they feared were in danger of imminent death or were otherwise unable to travel to the mission due to ill health” (19). Importantly, while they functioned to admit the baptized into the missionary system, such provisional baptisms were complemented with an additional baptismal ceremony. Again referring to the ECPP Guide, these ceremonies were performed “[at] a later date, if the ego survived,” at which point “the Franciscans would execute the complete rite of baptism, stating in the record that they had ‘supli las ceremonias,’ or in a crude translation, supplied the full ceremonies. It should be noted that this was not a second baptism, but the completion of the original baptism” (Guide for Users, 19). Cruzado‘s note that should Maria recover, she would receive the remaining ceremonies is a reference to this practice (“la que si convaleze recibira las dimas ceremonias”). That no date is included for this subsequent ceremony, and that her burial date of December 9th, 1777 closely follows the original event strongly suggests a delayed fatality directly related to her injuries sustained during the Bear encounter or secondary complications therefrom. Owing to a lack of further detail, the representative date assigned to this history reflects its latest possible occurrence (the date of baptism). Both Maria Liberata‘s previously-unbaptized status and her recorded origin of “rancheria Asuhsabit” should prompt consideration for this history's relationship to ancestral, seasonal energetic streams and the associated, genered labour roles of Tongva-Gabrieleño communities, particularly in light of their relationship to historical Kinship practices and human-Bear encounter in the San Gabriel Valley and foothills. While the precise date of Maria Liberata‘s encounter with the Bear is unknown, and the geography described as her point of origin (or at least, potentially, her locality at the time of the encounter) is neither causal nor definitive, Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) provides important context. The importance of ancestral acorn-gathering among the Tongva-Gabrieleño people is very well established, as are the gendered lines along which this labour fell: women, principally, were the keepers of this knowledge and central participants in the autumn acorn harvest (See, for example, Rosanne Welch, A Brief History of the Tongva Tribe, 2006, 7-8, 11). Considered alongside this context, the known localities both of Tongva-Gabrieleño village sites and keystone food processing locations (particularly those local to Beatty Canyon and Van Tassel Canyon on either side of Fish Canyon) lend support to the possibility that the San Gabriel foothills may be relevant to this encounter's geography. It is also important to note that mission San Gabriel Arcángel had only very recently moved to its second (and permanent) site two years prior in 1775, situating missionaries much closer to the foothills, potentially making the transportation of the injured or sick individuals to the mission (as is implied by Maria Liberata‘s baptismal location, in “esta mision”) more feasible than it had previously been. A representative location has been set based on this history. Maria Liberata‘s burial data denotes no spousal or familial relationships associated with San Gabriel Arcángel. Her baptismal record describes Maria as thirty five years old. T.GB.1777.1, Early California Population Project Database, Baptism number 00346, Burial number(s): 00064. descriptions.value: Ysidoro Barcenilla recorded the 25th April, 1800 death and 26th April burial of Tunque (Spanish name, Thomas), born c.1782, at the cemetery of the first chapel of Mission San José, stating of the eighteen year “comido un oso de medio cuerpo a bajo.“ Tunque’s baptismal record refers to his origin only as “Norte del.” A review of additional (digitized) baptismal records inclusive of this phrase which are specific to this mission, the years inclusive and prior to his baptism, and the padres local to baptismal operations in this region, the phrase “del norte” appears in conjunction with “capilla de esta mission” in the ECPP database. This is consistent both in records specific to Ysidoro Barcenilla and corroborated by those of Jose Antonio de Uria. Taken alongside Byrd et al.‘s 2018 analysis of baptismal trends for tribal communities within this gepgraphy in the final decade of the eighteenth century, and Engbring et al.‘s 2019 excavations, this history should be considered in dialogue with the history of at Síi Túupentak (CA-ALA-565/H), a protohistoric ancestral Ohlone village and burial site north of the mission site near the Alameda Creek and Arroyo de la Laguna confluence. The geography of Síi Túupentak is the most likely geographic and social relationship to Tunque’s baptism, death, and burial at the cemetery (likely, that of the mission). Because the specific site at which Tunque’s remains were found is not available, but a land relationship with both the mission area and Síi Túupentak are known or reasonably plausible, the representative geospatial data point assigned to this microhistory is situated in the Fremont Hills (foothills of the Diablo Range) to represent the confluence of mission lands and ancestral land relationships. Neither Tunque‘s burial nor baptismal data denote a spousal relationship. The rhetoric used by Barcenilla is not explicit enough to imply predation or scavenging. While compatibility alone is in itself insufficient towards providing a conclusive identification for the animal actor involved in this fatality event, the pattern of consumption described by Barcenilla warrants a conservative interpretation of this history. Although the record explicitly attributes Tunque’s death to a Bear, the restricted anatomical distribution and consumption pattern are potentially suggestive of a large felid. Particularly, the substantial consumption of bone, injury at the lower torso (potentially, beneath the ribs) and (potential) severing of the spine are biologically compatible with known aspects of mountain lion prey caches in early points of consumption. Though accuracy cannot be assumed, the stated time elapsed between the date of death indicated by the ECPP and subsequent burial one day later also supports pause, with felids capable of rapid carcass exploitation partly fitting this description. Though this data point will remain classified as ursine, because these aspects of the history produce reasonable doubt, and because felids and other top consumers are not referenced, this is a low confidence entry which will be revisited as more data becomes available. Should it become clear from future investigation that the attribution of this fatality to an ursine actor becomes erroneous, this data point will be shifted to a Tier 4 entry and a separate, corresponding  entry will be made with the most appropriate animal attribution for the Tier 1 aspect of the event. descriptions.value: Estevan Tapis recorded the death of Suayeuset (Francisco de Borja (Spanish name) “[near the tules],“ at or near Mission Santa Barbara in the first days of May, 1799. Of the encounter, Tapis writes: “certifico el infra-escrito Ministro de esta Mission de Sta Barbara que (segun noticia que han dado varios gentiles) en los primeros dias del mes de Mayo del año 1799 Francisco de Borja Suayeuset ... murio cerca de los Tulares, despedesado de un osso de cuyo cadaver no se hallo segun cuentan los mismos gentiles, mas que una mano...” (English: “I, the undersigned Minister of this Mission of Santa Barbara, certify that (according to reports that have been given by several gentiles) in the early days of May 1799, Francisco de Borja Suayeuset... died near the Tulares, torn apart by a bear[,] of his corpse—according to the accounts of those same Gentiles—nothing was found but a single hand…”). As indicated, Tapis acted only as recorder of Suayeuset‘s death, writing that his entry made on the 16th of May was relative to the death date “[en] los primeros dias del mes de Mayo,” and noting that he was informed of the death by an unknown multiple of non-baptized Indigenous individuals. That Tapis’s entry appears at minimum suggestive of a degree of disbelief aligns with known resistance landscapes specific to Santa Barbara. Read alongside the fact that Suayeuset‘s burial records reference his origin as “rancheria de Chnajalayegua,” a hispanicization of a Chumash village (Najalayegua, Shnaxalayiwis), suggests further entanglement with later, nineteenth century histories of cimarrones local to this region. A representative location has been set based on this history which is reflective of the tule to which the account refers. Suayeuset‘s burial data does not denote a spousal relationship associated with mission Santa Barbara. descriptions.value: Jose Espi recorded the September 3rd, 1798, burial of Primo (Spanish name) at “rancho de San Pedro,“ writing that his death was “de resultas de unas mordidas de un oso”. Although no officiant is specified, that Espi notes that Primo “recibidos los Santos Sacramentos” strongly suggests that Primo survived the initial encounter with the Bear, as last rites are administered to the living. We can therefore assume that the encounter occurred in late August or early September of 1798, and that Primo later passed from associated injuries, infection, or disease. The location to which Espi refers as Primo‘s burial site is San Pedro y San Pablo Asistencia, a sub-mission to San Francisco de Asís Mission and Presidio established c.1784 at the site of the Aramai village “Pruristac.” Pruristac’s history (also significant for its relationship with another Aramai village, Timigtac, located to the north on Calera Creek) is associated with forced labor conditions and limestone mining at Montara Mountain. A representative location has been set based on this history. Primo‘s burial data denotes a spousal relationship with “Cuarta” (Spanish name), also associated with San Francisco de Asís Mission and Presidio. descriptions.value: Josef Maria Fernandez officiated and recorded the May 10th death and May 11th, 1797 burial of Gregorio (Spanish name), of San Josef (Pueblo de San José de Guadalupe), writing that he was “despedazado de un osso.“ While the precise date of the encounter is known for this history, the location is not. A representative location has been set at the historic marker for the Pueblo de San José de Guadalupe (marker 433, erected by the California State Department of Parks and Recreation and the San Jose Historic Landmarks Commission in 1977). This microhistory‘s relationship to the third mission site for Santa Clara de Asís also calls to attention its potential relationship to the confluence of the Guadalupe River and The Alameda, a route rennovated by Franciscans in c.1795 to facilitate transportation between these two locations. Road infrastrucure has been tagged in association for this reason. Gregorio‘s burial data denotes a spousal relationship with “Juana Maria (Spanish name),” also associated with mission Santa Clara de Asís. descriptions.value: Pascual Martinez de Arenaza officiated and recorded the March 18th, 1797 burial of Lumenquens (Spanish name, Mansueto Jose Lumenquens), age 53 (born c.1744), of San Carlos Borromeo, writing “muerto por el oso“ at the “para[j]e Upfaaguano,“ (a location for which more information is currently unknown). The precise date of the encounter is not known, but that Arenaza notes that the burial was conducted during the same month as the death suggests that the encounter occurred between March 1st and March 17th, 1797. De Arenaza wrote that he ‘blessed the grave and performed the burial rite’ (“bendige el oyo y le hice el oficio de sepultura“) at “Upfaaguano.“ While his burial record refers to Lumenquens as being “de Ensen o Sanjones,” baptismal record denotes potential ancestral relationship to the “ranchería llamada Exen” (which the ECPP identifies as Eslenaj). Because the location of “Upfaaguano” is as yet difficult to determine, this data point presents the locality at which Fray. de Arenaza was stationed at this time as a representative location. Two distinct trajectories emerge when considering de Arenaza's departure from this site. In one, de Arenaza, months from retiring, would have travelled northeast toward the missionary frontier. In the other, Fray. de Arenaza would have travelled southeast, towards the victim’s (inferred) ancestral lands. Because each of these (likeliest) trajectories describe two distinct environments, each of which holds further, significant ethnographic context, an assumption on route cannot responsibly be made with available data. Lumenquens burial data denote a spousal relationship with “Parasebes Maria Jaccastus,” (potentially a blend of Indigenous and Franciscan naming conventions), whose records are also associated with San Carlos Borromeo. descriptions.value: The death and September 20th, 1793 burial of Tiriaci (Spanish name, Gaspar, b.c. 1740, baptism number 01745) at Mission Santa Clara de Asís as recorded by Thomas de la Peña refer to his having been “despedazado de un oso... el mismo dia.” Tiriaci was buried in the cemetery of the church at Santa Clara de Asís, with Thomas de la Peña acting as officiant and recorder. Tiriaci was the spouse of Pagmite (Spanish name, Cipriana, born c.1740 — December 2, 1798, baptism number 01765). Their marriage and nuptial blessing was performed in view of their pre-existing familial bond on August 17, 1790 by Diego de Noboa at Santa Clara de Asís (Marriage number: 00214). Records refer to two children baptized at Santa Clara de Asís whom Tiriaci and Pagmite shared: Benedicta (Spanish name, born c.1781 — c. June 28, 1792, baptism number 01740) and Evaristo (Spanish name, born c.1774 — c. December 2, 1798, baptism number 01749). A number of records pertaining to Tiriaci refer to San Carlos Borromeo as his origin and suggest the same of Pagmite. San Carlos Borromeo is also described as the origin of their eldest child, Evaristo. Santa Clara de Asís was founded on January 12th, 1777. The events in this microhistory align with the third site of mission Santa Clara de Asís ((1781)1784-1818). descriptions.value: “José Señán recorded the death and burial of Chalc (assigned the Spanish name Francisca Maria at baptism), an Indigenous woman of about twenty-five years of age at Mission San Carlos Borromeo as follows: “Francisca Maria (Chalc) [era] despedazada por los ossos (segun mas piamente se cree) ... cortonos de esta mision ... se recogieron todos los fracmentos q.e se pudo de su cadaver y fueron sepultados a la entrada de la Iglesia de esta mision [el diez de Noviembre, 1791]. Desde el num[er]o 831 hasta el ante. 845 esta corregido y con esta tacha valen.” English: “Francisca Maria (Chalc) was torn to pieces by the bears (according to what is more piously believed)… at the outskirts of this mission … they recovered all of the fragments that they could (pudo) of her body … buried at the entrance of the church of this mission [on the] 10th of November 1791.” José Señán recorded Chalc’s burial at the “entrada de la Iglesia” following the fatal encounter, but is not listed as an officiant thereof. Chalc is described as the spouse of Estanislao Jose Tupay (Spanish name). Juan Crespí baptized both her mother (Maria Francisca (Spanish name, baptism number 00031)) on December 31st, 1772 at paraje de la Playa when she was twenty nine years old, and her father (Felis / Felix Juan “El Ranchero” (Spanish name, baptism number 00130)) on the 22nd June 1773, when he was twenty eight. Chalc‘ s parents‘ and siblings‘ baptismal records, as well as her own, all denote their individual origins as “Tucutnnut alias la rancheria de Santa Thereza.” Baptism link mission number 00061, Burial number(s): 00833. T.GB.1791.1, Early California Population Project Database. Content notice: engage this history with respect and care. descriptions.value: Miguel Sanchez recorded the death and burial of Florentina Gertrudis of Mission San Gabriel Arcángel as follows: “mataron los osos” [en] “el campo.” Sanchez writes that, inferrably owing to circumstance, Florentina was unable to receive last sacrament. Florentina's baptismal record denotes her origin as “rancheria [de] Cucamobit,” a reference which should be taken in dialogue with a number of known Gabrielino-Tongva settlement and community sites, including Cucamonga (see: Sam Villa, Villages, tongvapeople (dot) org; Villarreal et al., “Analysis of a Middle Period Site at Little Red Hill in Rancho Cucamonga.”). She was buried May 9th, 1786, roughly two months after her baptism on March 3rd, 1786 at the Church of San Gabriel Arcángel. Florentina was listed as being twenty years old at the time of her baptism, suggesting a potential birth date c.1766. Miguel Sanchez officiated and recorded Florentina’s burial in the church cemetery. Baptism number: 01311, Burial number(s): 00435. T.GB.1786.1, Early California Population Project Database. descriptions.value: “Indios de esta mission Gregoria Maria (n.c.1759-m.1779, veinte años, Bap: 00288), (esposa de) Ignacio (o Ygnacio) Maria (n.c.1763-m.1812, Bap: 00070) (y sus) hijo, Antonio Maria ((n. 7 de Junio, 1779 - 8 de Sieptiembre, 1779), Bap: 00497) hallaron muertos en esta Mission como media legua distante, io mas del comida de los animales. (Gregoria Maria y su hijo era) de Adjuibit. Enterrado en el cementerio de esta mission. Antonio Cruzado.“ T.U.1779.1, Burial number(s): 00099 and 00100, Early California Population Project Database. On September 8th, 1779, the bodies of Gregoria Maria and her the three month old son, Antonio Maria, were found approximately one and a half (modern) miles from the grounds of the San Gabriel Arcángel mission (modern-day San Gabriel, California). The condition of their remains led Antonio Paterna, officiant to and recorder of the burials for both, to indicate that they had been “largely consumed by animals.” Gregoria was twenty years old, originally native to Awingna (Awizna, Awig-na, Awigna), a Tongva-Gabrieleño settlement twelve miles east of an Gabriel Arcángel near modern La Puente, California (see: Sam Villa, Villages, tongvapeople (dot) org). She was married to Ignacio (Ygnacio) Maria, originally from the settlement of Pomoquin, with whom she lived at San Gabriel Arcángel. The extent to which this record implies a relationship with scavenging or prey caching behavior is unclear, and no further information on associated species can be discerned from available records at this time. descriptions.value: “Mr. George Spurr, who was recently engaged at mining on Sutter Creek, was of a party who succeeded in catching a grizzly bear in a steel trap. While they were trying to lasso the bear to get entire command of him, Mr. Spurr happened to get within reach of the beast’s jaws, and had his arm very severely bitten. descriptions.value: “Sacramento City, April 8 1851. Friend Ewer: Pursuant to promise, I now proceed to indite a few lines for the ‘Nevada Journal,’ of which I have the honor of being the original projector, but owing to a combination of circumstances, I was unable to carry through as I anticipated. descriptions.value: “As a company of packers and disappointed miners from Scott’s River, were crossing over from the Sacramento to Feather River, on Saturday last, they fell in with a Grizzley, near Babcock’s rancho, on the latter river, about fourteen miles from this place. A couple of ex-officio sailors, a German by the name of Schultz, and a Spanish vaquero gave chase; and after a brisk run of two miles across an open plain, they came upon him near a large thicket of chaparral. The only gun in the company, a doable-barreled shot gun, loaded with buck shot was fired broad side at him with no other apparent affect than a growl upon the part of old bruin. — The ‘bar’ then concealed himself amid the dense chaparral, whereupon Shultz dismounted, and with cocked revolver in band entered the thicket, creeping along on ‘all fours’ — determined to seek out his bearship’s whereabouts or ‘die trying.’ But his courage and curiosity both received a sudden chill by the appearance of Mr. Grizzly, who, with an angry growl, rushed upon the daring intruder into his private walks — biting him frightfully on the left arm, and lacerating him severely in the back, and other parts, with his monstrous claws. But upon Schultz’s crying ‘enough,’ and the clamors of the rest of the party — two of whom were unhorsed at the onset of this last attack — the bear seized the hat of the fallen combatant as a trophy of his victory, and shaking it with savage spitefulness, toddled off, while his inglorious pursuers very judiciously took an opposite direction, thoroughly satisfied with grizzly hunting. The bear was followed next morning by Dr. Frazier, of this place, Mr. Babcock and several others — all well armed, who tracked him to the Buttes, but did not succeed in routing him. Schultz was brought into town and his wounds were dressed by Dr. Pierce. The bear was said to be as large as a common mule — was very fat and was judged to weigh near 1400 pounds.“ T.GB.1851.3, Attack of a Bear - Men nearly killed!, Marysville Daily Herald, Volume I, Number 77, 10 April 1851. descriptions.value: “Captain Lewis H. Childs called on us yesterday evening, and exhibited several handsome specimens of gold. One of them was in shape an almost faultless boat, and was worth $91. A lump was taken from the same canon some time ago, which weighed four and a half pounds. The canon is three and a half miles long, and rich the entire extent. It is about 25 miles north-east of Georgetown, and close to the Middle Fork of the American River. Claims have been sold at times at extravagant prices, Capt. C. having bought one recently for which he gave $6,000. In October last, he sold a claim there for $20, out of which $13,000 has been taken already. The miners on Mad Canon are making from $16 to $150, except those who have not as yet got down to the bottom rock—such are making $5 per day. The gold lies deep, as twenty feet of earth must be excavated before they reach the bed rock. There are about two thousand miners in the vicinity, all of whom are making fair wages. Provisions are somewhat scarce. Flour is worth 20 a 25, pork 35 a 40, hams 45, potatoes 30 cents per pound. There is an abundance of deer a few miles off, which keeps the market pretty well supplied with fresh meat. Occasionally a grizzly is brought in by way of variety.“ GB.1851.5, Mad Canon Diggings, Sacramento Transcript, Volume 2, Number 120, 15 March 1851. descriptions.value: “Messrs. Editors: Nevada City, in most respects unique, presents to the stranger many features of absorbing interest. Far up towards the summit of the Sierra Nevada, where a few months ago the grizzly bear was undisturbed in his haunts, a populous city is now seen, its numerous streets compactly built, extending up rugged and narrow ravines, and over ridges ungraded, while the primitive forest in its native majesty still waves its proud coronal of evergreen far above the scene of bustling life below. The stranger as he retires for his first night’s repose, and is lulled to sleep by the music of the winds, sighing among the branches of the forest trees, 150 or 200 feet above his head, can scarcely realise that he is in the midst of an active, business population, as great as that of Sacramento City; yet the discoherent sounds issuing from a neighboring saloon, when a company of midnight revelers ‘are making night hideous’ with their bacchanalian orgies, forcibly reminds him that he is still amidst the habitations of civilized men. Nevada is particularly interesting as being in the midst of perhaps, one of the very richest mining districts in all California. Here probably the miner has been more uniformly successful than in any other portion of the gold region. While some, perhaps many, have realized their highest anticipations, a large portion of those who have been operating here, have met with a fair remuneration for their labor. No single locality presents so favorable an opportunity for observing mining operations in their various forms as Nevada. Here within a very short distance almost every variety of diggings are seen.“ T.GB.1850.21, Mining Operations in the North, Sacramento Transcript, Volume 2, Number 57, 31 December 1850. descriptions.value: “Mr. Pearson, who resides some thirty miles west of this city, brought into market yesterday, a wagon load of wild meats. An old grizzly with three cubs, together with a dozen of deer. Mr. P. states that grizzlies may be found in the tules ten miles west of the city, as also an abundance of deer. He is an excellent hunter, and is realizing a good deal of money by his attention to this pursuit. The game bro’t to this city was killed by himself and sons since Friday last. He had about five hundred pounds of deer meat which is worth twenty cents a pound, and this would rate him $100. The three cubs would weigh about one hundred and twenty pounds, and the old bear three hundred and fifty — which, at fifty cents a pound, yielded him $235. descriptions.value: “We commence, to-day, the publication of the favors of our correspondents at Umpqua City, and the Upper Valley of that fine stream. The entire region of Northern California and Southern Oregon, till within the past six months, was a terra incognito ; none knew of the noble and navigable streams since discovered and explored almost to their sources, or of the lovely and fertile valleys watered by them. We see in this extension of topographical knowledge, by which new avenues of enterprise and wealth are opened to our citizens, an indication of what is to be the future of the wonderful Empire arising and spreading along the shores of the vast Pacific. We have some valuable letters from Mr. Scholfield, giving the results of his own explorations; and we are promised by Col. H. Winchester a series of articles more fully treating upon the aspect and resources of the opened in a remarkable degree through his indomitable perseverence. The very crowded state of our columns precludes us from giving but a single letter this morning. Umpqua City, Oregon, Nov. 19,1850. Editors of the Pacific News : Having had my attention called to the report of the Klamath Exploring Expedition, in your paper, some time since, I was induced to visit a region of country of a character so promising. It gives me pleasure to say, in respect to that report, that it represented in modest terms the advantages and high prospects of the Umpqua river and valley. I have since the evidence of observation to confirm the' truth of its fullest statements. A safer harbor cannot be found, than this port offers, and with the aid of the charts, which are now in the hands of Winchester, Paine & Co., at San Francisco, the entrance is passed in security and with facility. The site of this place is level, and with an abundance of good timber in its immediate vicinity, there is no lack of building material. The river is, on either side, for forty miles, more heavily wooded with the finest timber, for lumber and other uses, that any country can boast. Above Scottsburg, which is situated at the head of navigation, the country begins to open into small and rich prairies, until we reach the valley of the Umpqua, where the broad, green plains fill the eye with their rolling meadows and shady groves, and present a virgin soil, such as must please the most fastidious agriculturist. I do not exaggerate, when I state that in two years, there will not be a good claim in this whole valley unoccupied. The settlers on the Columbia river, and in the Willammette valley, have, in numerous instances, sold their previous locations, and emigrated to this region—induced to do so by the fact that the soil is better, and the climate milder. Emigrants returning from California, overland, are locating here every day. The emigration by sea from your port has been considerable. The Reindeer, from San Francisco, and bound to Portland, stopped here a few days since, and left with us one-half of her passengers. This river is the nearest and only outlet to the rich valley in which it takes its source. The agricultural produce and lumber of this valley will find a ready market in California, which must give an impulse of a permanent character to this port. I have not yet visited the gold regions of this valley, but several parties are now forming for the purpose of mining, and with the highest hopes of success. Labor is in demand at California prices. Game of every kind found in abundance—geese, ducks, salmon, and shell-fish are furnished us in great numbers, by the Indians, for a small compensation. Bears, both black and grizzly, deers and elk, fill the hills and forests, and reward the exertions of whoever will take the pains to hunt them. There is at present a scarcity of provisions on the river. Pork, flour, sugar, beef, and other staple articles, command an advance of one hundred per cent, upon San Francisco prices. Clothing, boots and shoes, axes, and tools generally, are in demand. A shipment of such articles would be a remunerating investment. Several houses are already established here, and are doing a good business. I have endeavored to give you a brief description of this region, without exaggeration, and have withheld praise rather than added any color to truth. Should you wish to learn further particulars, I would refer you to Col. H. Winchester, who has a perfect knowledge of the country, and to whose intelligence and enterprise, all are indebted for the location and improvement of this important river. Respectfully yours, Samuel S. Mann.“ BB.1850.1, Our Umpqua Correspondence, Daily Pacific News, Volume II, Number 130, 26 December 1850. I do not exaggerate, when I state that in two years, there will not be a good claim in this whole valley unoccupied. The settlers on the Columbia river, and in the Willammette valley, have, in numerous instances, sold their previous locations, and emigrated to this region—induced to do so by the fact that the soil is better, and the climate milder. Emigrants returning from California, overland, are locating here every day. The emigration by sea from your port has been considerable. The Reindeer, from San Francisco, and bound to Portland, stopped here a few days since, and left with us one-half of her passengers. This river is the nearest and only outlet to the rich valley in which it takes its source. The agricultural produce and lumber of this valley will find a ready market in California, which must give an impulse of a permanent character to this port. I have not yet visited the gold regions of this valley, but several parties are now forming for the purpose of mining, and with the highest hopes of success. Labor is in demand at California prices. Game of every kind found in abundance—geese, ducks, salmon, and shell-fish are furnished us in great numbers, by the Indians, for a small compensation. Bears, both black and grizzly, deers and elk, fill the hills and forests, and reward the exertions of whoever will take the pains to hunt them. There is at present a scarcity of provisions on the river. Pork, flour, sugar, beef, and other staple articles, command an advance of one hundred per cent, upon San Francisco prices. Clothing, boots and shoes, axes, and tools generally, are in demand. A shipment of such articles would be a remunerating investment. Several houses are already established here, and are doing a good business. I have endeavored to give you a brief description of this region, without exaggeration, and have withheld praise rather than added any color to truth. Should you wish to learn further particulars, I would refer you to Col. H. Winchester, who has a perfect knowledge of the country, and to whose intelligence and enterprise, all are indebted for the location and improvement of this important river. Respectfully yours, Samuel S. Mann.“ T.GB.1850.20, Our Umpqua Correspondence, Daily Pacific News, Volume II, Number 130, 26 December 1850. descriptions.value: “Mountain game are beginning to come down from their summer haunts, and miners in various quarters of the State will be able to supply themselves with all kinds of wild meats. During the last season, quite a number of miners were able to keep themselves in fresh meat, and that of the choicest kind, without expending a dollar. We have had in market for some time past an abundance of venison and elk, and on several occasions a few haunches of the grizzly. The latter is regarded by many as one of the sweetest and most delicate meats. On the prairies antelopes are found in droves, and the wary huntsman not unfrequently makes a large haul during a single expedition. Several sportsmen made their piles last season by hunting; and we recollect of seeing a wagon enter our city regularly every morning, containing from three to five elk. In addition to the mountain game, our rivers afford a large supply of the finny tribe. The salmon and salmon trout appear to be the general favorites. The latter is taken in large quantities twenty miles, and probably higher up the American river. The abrupt falls, however, prevent these fish being found near the sources of our streams; although noted for their leaping power, they are compelled to “cave” when they attempt to scale some of the precipitous points found in our rivers. We understand that the Merced abounds with millions of salmon at this time, and that many persons are now engaged in taking and curing them for winter use. One man, it is said, can with a spear alone, take a thousand pounds per day of these delicious fish. If this is correct, the miners will need far less supplies of meat and fish than formerly.“ GB.1850.21, California Game, Sacramento Transcript, Volume 2, Number 31, 29 November 1850. descriptions.value: “These ravines are very numerous, but none are of great length, as they all head west of the Sacramento road, below Auburn, and run off laterally, emptying into the large ravine. Our company were amongst the first who located here, but now we have plenty of neighbors, and the white covers of log cabins can be seen in all directions. Game is moderately abundant, and in the absence of water for working our machines, a good portion of our time is spent in traversing the hills down to the plains. One Mr. Brown wandered so at random, not long since, that he had to pass an inclement night as sentinel over the cayotas. He told us he had been hunting grizzly bears, but he brought in no game. There is one evil existing around us of such a grievous nature, that it ought to be kept so continually before the people, that every man will bear it in mind. It has been growing long enough, and it is time it was removed, root and branch. I refer to the stealing of horses, mules and cattle.— There are a great number of unprincipled scoundrels, too lazy to labor, who are picking up all the stock they can find; and no miner around us can turn out his animal, but what, in less than twenty-four hours, it is run off where the chances are, he will never find it again. Our animals, to the number of some half a dozen, have all disappeared, and the probabilities are we shall see them no more.“ T.GB.1850.18, Interesting from the Diggings, Sacramento Transcript, Volume 2, Number 45, 16 December 1850. descriptions.value: “Mr. Brooks of Nevada City, in company with an Indian boy, who is in his employ, were out on a hunting excursion a few days ago, on Bear River, in the vicinity of Steep Hollow, and when least expecting it, a huge grizzly bear pounced out upon them from a pile of brush. Mr. Brooks was first beset by the ferocious stranger, and narrowly escaped by taking refuge behind a tree. The bear then attacked the boy in a most violent manner, tearing the whole cheek from one side of his face, and lacerating, in a shocking manner, on of his arms and thigh. After a warm contest, Mr. Brooks drove off the bear. The boy was conveyed home, and, at last accounts, was scarcely expected to survive his wounds. Next day, a party set out in pursuit of Bruin, overtook and succeeded in dispatching him, after a sanguinary battle. He weighed, when dressed, eight hundred pounds.“ GB.1850.20, An Encounter with a Bear, Marysville Daily Herald, Volume I, Number 36, 6 December 1850.
