descriptions.value: “A few days since, I paid a flying visit to Stockton, the entrepot for the Southern Mines. At 4 p. m., I took my departure in the new steamer Erastus Corning, built by Messrs Morton, Lighthall and others. — For her size, she is without exception the most comfortable boat I ever travelled in, sitting like a duck on the water without the slightest vibration of motion. We were soon threading our way through the crowd of shipping that fills our noble harbor, and met a ship under sail just in from sea, and as we went by she seemed in the majesty of her cloud of canvas to say who will dispute with me the dominion of the ocean. On her quarter deck stood the pilot, his thoughtful countenance showing the heavy responsibility he felt in bringing her and her precious cargo into such a crowded port. Soon we cleared the shipping, passing the magnificent steamer N. World, the leviathan of the rivers, as she lay at her wharf sending forth angry puffs of steam as though impatient to start. Angel island, the Brothers, Sisters, Benicia, New York, &c., passed in rapid succession, and morning found us safely moored at Stockton. I was soon on shore and in the midst of a busy throng of teamsters, miners, &c., hurrying to and fro, and giving undoubted proof that the southern mines are in the full tide of successful operation. I spent the first part of the day in visiting every part of this wonderful emporium, sprung into existence as it were in a night, like the palace of Aladdin in the Arabian nights. Mr. Weaver's princely mansion, the improving row of buildings in which the Post Office is contained, and the grand hotel, are edifices which can take their places alongside many of our old city buildings on the Atlantic coast. I doubt not but that another year will see Stockton trebled in size at least. The slough on which the city stands swarms with fish, so I was tempted to try my luck with the finny tribe. I soon bought some lines, and hooks and started down the shore in a boat with two brother anglers to fish for our dinners. Whether we were unskilful or not, is not for us to say, but the perch leaped around us and seemed to laugh at us as we sat in a leaky old boat making great exertions to keep our clothes from being soiled and our boots from taking in too much water. A party of fishermen drawing a seine, passed just then and a few silver hooks soon filled our receptacle for game, and we returned to our friends where by keeping dark we obtained an enviable reputation for skill and wonderful appetites. On my way, I saw a large specimen of the grizzly in the road, and was pleased to find a chain around his neck, the other end being fast to a post, otherwise a clean pair heels would have been my only chance.“ GB.1850.19, Communicated, Daily Alta California, Volume 1, Number 285, 13 November 1850. descriptions.value: “A gentleman who resides near Sonoma, was on a deer hunt a few days ago, and when separated from his companions, discovered something in a thicket, which he supposed to be a deer. But on approaching, a loud growl showed him that he had waked up the wrong passenger. Withdrawing a space, he posted himself on an eminence overlooking the thicket, and there prepared himself with his rifle, having his horse standing by in case of need. When opportunity offered, he fired and struck the animal. On the instant a second huge bear leapt forth, and attacked the wounded beast, and the two had a furious grapple, while our friend was reloading his rifle. In a few moments, however, they parted, and the uninjured hear slowly approached the gentleman and took a deliberate survey of him, and then as composedly walked off, while the wounded bear hid himself in the bushes. Waiting some time, our friend cautiously entered the thicket, and at length found poor bruin stretched out quietly, with his paws over his face. Whether dead or alive he could not discover. He fired again, but owing to agitation or some other cause, entirely missed his aim. Bruin, however, was not to be disturbed—he was in the sleep of death, killed by a single shot, which is a very rare occurrence. The ball had severed the main artery below the heart, causing him to bleed to death. The animal was in fine order, and afforded excellent fare for the hunter and his guests.“ T.GB.1850.12, Grizzly Bear, Marysville Daily Herald, Volume I, Number 28, 8 November 1850. descriptions.value: “We give the following letters from two gentlemen who were on board the ill-fated vessel at the time of the explosion. They estimate the number on board, it will be seen, as much greater than some of the officers of the vessel have done: Editors of Alta California: — We, the undersigned, being on board the Steamer Sagamore at the time of the explosion, deem it our duty to state to the public, so far as in our power, the particulars of this awful occurrence. I (Jas. Kirker,) had just got on board and was going aft to pay my passage, when the explosion took place, and was thrown some ten or fifteen feet in the air, and lit on the bodies of two persons (dead). When I recovered my presence of mind, and the steam had cleared away, I saw as many as twenty-five persons on deck, who were apparently not hurt, and a great many who were either killed or very badly wounded. I saw two hanging on the side of the wreck, badly wounded and crying for help. I caught hold and pulled them in. By this time several boats had got alongside and were busy picking up those who were thrown into the water. As I was so late getting on board, I therefore knew nothing of what was transpiring on board. I should think there were as many as 130 persons on the upper deck when the explosion took place. I have been in the Rocky Mountains since 1821, trapping beaver and killing grizzly bears, and for the last five years fighting the Apaches and other hostile tribes, as well as being Col. Doniphan’s guide, spy and interpreter from Santa Fe to Matamoros. So that I have seen some service as well as being in some tight places, but this being blown sky high by a little hot water, and I so mixed up that it was very uncertain how I would come down, (O. K. was very uncertain,) is more than I have been accustomed to, and in future I shoulder old “Reality,” and take Walker's line, driving tandem, (i. e. one foot before the other,) in preference to traveling on these blow up concerns.“ GB.1850.15, The Sagamore, Daily Alta California, Volume 1, Number 272, 31 October 1850. descriptions.value: “We have received the following note from the renowned “Bear Hunter” of San Francisco, and in accepting his apology for past offences of omission, we have half a mind to do the same by those of commission, that is, dine with him to-day, not only on account of the savory viands with which his larder is stored, but for the pleasure of listening to a farther recital of his ‘grizzly’ adventures. At the present writing, we are inclined to think we’ll take the stories and the bar meat at the same tint’, to-day at one o’clock. Editor of Pacific News: “My Dear Sir—l have to offer a thousand apologies for neglecting to invite you to the dinner given the corps editorial at the Ontario House, on Tuesday last, and as many thanks for the handsome manner in which you reminded me of that neglect, through the columns of your paper to-day. The fact is, when we met a few days ago at Mrs. Graham’s, I was not aware that I had the honor of breakfasting with the Editor of the Pacific News, otherwise I would most cordially have extended to him the invitation which had already been extended to the other editors of my acquaintance. Under the circumstances, I trust the Editor of the Pacific News will do me the favor to dine with me at the Ontario to-mor-row, precisely at 1 o’clock, P. M., when, I assure him, it will afford me much pleasure to continue the account of my bear hunting excursions, and become better acquainted with him. I feel myself under obligations to the gentlemen who conduct the press in San Francisco, for the many favorable notices they have been pleased to take of my endeavors to establish a house worthy of public patronage, and I assure them that it will be both my pleasure and pride, and that I shall spare neither trouble nor expense to keep a house that will not disappoint the expectations raised by such generous and flattering announcements. Respectfully Yours, Bear Hunter.“ GB.1850.14, The Bear Hunter, Daily Pacific News, Volume II, Number 72, 18 October 1850. descriptions.value: “‘The Mound Rock’ is the heading of a short article in the Illustrated California News, which describes a singular natural elevation, or table rock, covering an area of some acres, which is to be found at Mr. Scott’s ranch on the Mercedes river. We might incline to the opinion of the writer in the News, that this is artificial, were it not perfectly evident from the dip of the strata which compose this singular mound, that it is not the work of masonry, but of the upheaval of some pent-up forces in the earlier geological periods [of] the planet. This opinion is still further confirmed by the fact that these exist on the plain between Scott’s ranch and the foot hills of the Tuolumne—say covering a space of ten or fifteen miles square —numberless more of these singular mounds, which we are satisfied, also, are not artificial. They are situated some miles from the nearest of the main road leading from Stockton to the Mariposa, and we should never have met them had not curiosity taken us across that portion of the ‘painted prairie’ in April last. To effect a cut-off, also, was in part an object. We steered by compass from the upper (Texan) ferry of the Mercedes, to Jackson’s ranch, (Horr’s ferry,) on the Tuolumne. About midway on this journey, we were overtaken by night, and having the fear of a grizzly before our eyes, we climbed one of the mounds, and with a blanket, there slept in the moon’s pale cold light.“ T.GB.1849.7, Curious Geological Phenomena, Daily Pacific News, Volume II, Number 69, 15 October 1850. descriptions.value: “Our streets have been enlivened every evening for a few days back, by regular stump speeches from the several candidates for office. A large audience is easily gathered. All the speaker has to do is, down with a box, or end a barrel, and mount. Sometimes a crowd is easily pleased—at other times they are cross, ill-grained—then woe to him who does not meet and answer questions plumply. There is one candidate however, who stands par excellence, with all sorts of people, with all classes of the community,—one who never fails to give satisfaction to his crowd, and who always comes off more than conqueror—that man is the inimitable, the famed Capt. Thomas Spikens. Tom had a merry crowd of the b’hoys around him last evening, and held forth somewhat in the following strain: “Feller Citizens: I shall now cum rite out with my sentimens on the Squatter question. There ain’t nary one of my opponents who’s got the pluck to come to the pint — they git mitey close to it, like a moth, to a lighted candle, but about the time it feels hot, away they go, makin’ a orful buzzin’ and flapping of wings [...] You want my sentimens on Taxes. Well I go in strong for reducin’ the Taxes, and if you elect me, which I ‘spec’ you will, I shall propose right oft’ reducin’ all salaries to seventy five dollars a month and boarded cheap — likker three times a day, and pipes and tobiiker throw’d in — a heavy premium on wolf and grizzly scalps, and an appropriation for a fence to keep the bullocks off the coons.“ T.GB.1850.9, Political Movements - Tom Spikens, Sacramento Transcript, Volume 1, Number 134, 5 October 1850. descriptions.value: “On the 23d inst., while Mr. Walker, of Louisiana, and a companion were out on a gunning excursion, the former walking off alone, saw a she bear and two cubs; to get out of her way he ascended a tree, and after she had left he came down, and after passing on some distance he again encountered the animal; she immediately attacked him, and while he was attempting to fire into her mouth she struck the gun to one side, and it exploded without injuring her. He then drew a small sheath knife and defended himself with it until it broke off. After throwing him about some time with her teeth and claws she left him. He was found by a party set out after him, about 200 yards from the spot where the bear attacked him. His wounds, we regret to say, are of a very serious character; a deep cut from one claw cutting entirely through the muscles under the left arm, another deep gash close to the femoral artery in the left thigh extends for three inches, and another for several inches from the top of the forehead down between the eyes. Numerous other wounds of both teeth and claws mark the ferocious character of the grisly bear as one of the most dangerous in the world. The suffering man bears all without complaint: he is under the care of Dr. Davis B. Cassiday, and doing well, and though occasionally delirious, will probably recover.“ T.GB.1850.8B, Ferocity of a Bear, Daily Alta California, Volume 1, Number 258, 16 October 1850. He then drew a small sheath knife and defended himself with it until it broke off. After throwing him about some time with her teeth and claws she left him. He was found by a party set out after him, about 200 yards from the spot where the bear attacked him. His wounds, we regret to say, are of a very serious character; a deep cut from one claw cutting entirely through the muscles under the left arm, another deep gash close to the femoral artery in the left thigh extends for three inches, and another for several inches from the top of the forehead down between the eyes. Numerous other wounds of both teeth and claws mark the ferocious character of the grisly bear as one of the most dangerous in the world. The suffering man bears all without complaint: he is under the care of Dr. Davis B. Cassiday, and doing well, and though occasionally delirious, will probably recover.“ T.GB.1850.8A, Ferocity of a Bear, Daily Alta California, Volume 1, Number 258, 16 October 1850. descriptions.value: “We are informed that last Sunday evening, a grizzly bear entered the corn-field of the Indians living on their rancharie, situated on Tuolumne river, just below Claxton & Horr’s ferry. It was about 12 o’clock at night, and a party of the Indians, with their squaws, were watching their corn and salmon fishery situated in the neighborhood. At the time the bear entered the field, the Indians were asleep and bruin went to the fish pen. stole a large salmon, and walking down he river a short distance, stopped to regale himself on the fish in the immediate neighborhood of a sleeping squaw, who was awakened by him and shouted for help. The bear dropped the fish and darted at the squaw, who was most dreadfully bitten and torn by the monster. A shout resounded in every part of the rancheria, and the whole party in a few moments were on their way to the scene of the catastrophe, armed with bows and arrows, but the bear eluded their pursuit by running into a thick chaparral.“ T.GB.1850.7, Grizzly Bear, Sacramento Transcript, Volume 1, Number 122, 21 September 1850. descriptions.value: “The bars in this neighborhood bear rather terrible names to the verdant diggers, and from the questions asked on their arrival, you would judge their stay depended upon your replies. We have Murderer's Bar, Dead Man's Bar, and Rattlesnake Bar, and with each of these bars is connected some horrible legend, which has given the above sanguinary titles to them. A few miles above us there is a deep gulch, where, last winter, among others, was encamped a timid juvenile, who had a holy horror of Indian yells, grizzly roars, and even coyote barks. A waggish neighbor, being aware of the amiable weakness of the youth, maliciously took advantage of his failing, and one night managed so to combine all the above noises, as to give utterance to the most demoniacal and hideous sounds ever heard in this land of originalities. The performer being located near the young man’s abode, the consequences were very much as anticipated. Terrified and panic stricken, the digger vamosed the ranch, clothed in nothing but his flannel, and dug up the hill as he never dug before. The red ensign was discovered early the ensuing morning near the summit of the hill, but its former proprietor had entirely disappeared, rigged in Georgia costume, sans the spurs. Since that memorable night of that wonderful flight, the ravine has gone by the appropriate appellation (although perhaps not clothed in sufficient words) of “Shirttail Canon.” It has not proved as bare as its name would seem to indicate, for many have been wholly suited by a few weeks, residence there. I must not omit to state that the flighty flannel is hoisted upon a pole in front of the store, and it serves as a beacon light to the weary digger, who has been walking all day in order to reach the far-famed “Shirt-tail Canon.” T.GB.1849.5, Sacramento Transcript, Volume 1, Number 39, 15 June 1850. descriptions.value: “The territory of California possesses almost every variety of climate. In the vallies near the coast, spring and summer reign perpetually. The more elevated parts near the mountain tops change from summer’s melting heat to that of winter’s chilling cold. Immediately on the coast the fury of the broad Pacific’s winds keep present almost perpetually Autumn's bracing temperature. The soil of some of the vallies is equal to the richest we have seen in the most fertile portions of the United States, and the remainder is not inferior to the generality of the productive portions of that country. The present vegetable productions are wheat, barley, oats, (wild) corn, potatoes, peas, beans, cabbage, onions, turnips, beets, parsnips, tomatoes, radishes, lettuce, cucumbers, pumpkins, melons, &c. Hemp is found growing wild; cotton is as yet an experiment. The fruits are apples, pears, peaches, nectarines, quinces, figs, prunes, olives, oranges, lemons, grapes, &c. Animals—horses, beef cattle, sheep and goats (local,), grizzly, brown and black bear, elk, deer, antelope, raccoon, rabbit, squirrel, panther, black wolf, prairie wolf, badger, &c. Fish—sturgeon, salmon, mackerel, herring, trout, perch, shark and porpoise, &c. Fowls—geese, ducks, brants, pelicans, swans and a great variety of small birds. Minerals—gold silver, quicksilver, copper. Lead and coal, but little discovered. descriptions.value: “Col. Fremont's Geographical Memoir on Upper California thus speaks of the climate of the gold region: The gold region of California is on the Sacramento river and its tributaries. The climate of the country has no winter in the valley, but the rainy season and the dry. The rainy season begins in November and continues to the middle of February or the beginning of March; the rest of the year is without rain; but the streams from the Sierra Nevada afford all the facilities for irrigation in the heats of July and August. The whole valley abounds in wild cattle, wild horses, elks, deer, antelopes, grizzly bears, partridges, water-fowI, salmon, &c. All the products of the United States, from apples to oranges, from potatoes to sugarcane, may be produced in the valley of the San Joaquin and Sacramento. The climate is remarkably healthy. Such is the California on the Pacific; the richest, most picturesque and beautiful region, for its extent, upon the face of the earth Such is the Eldorado of the gold mines; such is the great acquisition of the late war with Mexico. The California gold-finding scheme turns out, it is said, to be merely a hoax or rather, a delusion. The imaginary gold is but a very common valueless mineral, yellow mica. Many of our early voyagers were deceived the same way. Liverpool Mercury. That will be news indeed when it reaches California. Those who cannot tell yellow mica from gold could hardly find their way to that out-of-the-way country. Perhaps when the “Wilmot Proviso” extends to California, the gold miners will become more enlightened — New York Sun, The California Gold.” The California Gold, Weekly Alta California, 1 March, 1849. descriptions.value: “A Great Vision made Reality. In 1841 a very distinguished orator, in the Senate of the United States, in a speech upon the Pre-emption Bill, uttered the following prophetic language. What was prediction then, is about to become history now. “If to the other ties that bind us together as one people, he superadded the powerful interest springing out of' a just administration of our exhaustless public domain —by which, for a long succession of ages, in seasons of peace, the states will enjoy the benefit of the great and growing revenue which it produces, and in periods of war that revenue will be applied to the prosecution of the war—we shall be forever linked together with the strength of adamantine chains. No section, no state, would ever be mad enough to break off from the Union, and deprive itself of the inestimable advantages which it secures. Although thirty or forty more of the new states should be admitted into this Union, this measure would cement them all fast together. The honorable member from Missouri near me, (Mr. Linn,) is very anxious to have a settlement formed at the mouth of the Oregon, and he will probably be satisfied at no very distant day. Then will be seen members from the Pacific States scaling the Rocky Mountains, passing the country of the grizzly bear, descending the turbid Missouri, entering the father of rivers, ascending the beautiful Ohio, and coming to this capitol to take their seats in its spacious and magnificent halls. Proud of the commission they bear, and happy to find themselves here in council with friends and brothers and countrymen, enjoying the incalculable advantages of the great confederacy, and among them their annual distributive share of the is sues of a nation’s inheritance, would even they, the remote people of the Pacific, ever desire to separate themselves from such a high and glorious destiny?”.” A Great Vision Made Reality, Daily Pacific News, 15 November, 1849. descriptions.value: “The news from the mines, of which I have dates of but a few hours past, is quite encouraging. Miners, generally, are doing tolerably well. Some new gulches have been opened which promise to be as rich as Sullivan’s was; and probably is as rich as any that have been previously discovered. There has been a report quite prevalent here for several days past, and generally believed, that a gulch recently opened by three men, 20 miles eastward of the Sonoranian camp, yielded, in three days work, twenty-seven pounds of gold! Another report is that a gulch opened on the Stanislaus river, was yielding, to the lucky miners, eight, ten and twelve ounces per day! These reports have no substantiated authority, but I learned, in a conversation with a gentleman just down from Woods’s Diggings, that he, in part, accredited the latter report from information given him by a friend, in whom he places the greatest confidence. The health of the miners is very good; and, as near as I can learn, the miners are wearing away the winter very comfortably and profitably, notwithstanding the high price of everything requisite to sustain life. Many of them have built log cabins and are enjoying their dishes of venison, grizzly bear and other game; and all, who have come from the mines recently, give their preference to a residence in the mountains during the winter, to a locality in this place or San Francisco. The large streams and creeks have been temporarily abandoned by the miners in quest of dry diggings, and it will be not at all surprising, if before Spring, the people of the country are electrified with accounts of richer diggings than even the most credulous have entertained an idea of. descriptions.value: “Game. — Game is now very abundant in the vicinity of this place, particular upon the marshes, skirting the line of the Bay. Hunting, we think from the quantity of birds killed and brought into town, must be a good “paying” business. Sunday last, Messrs. Smith and Sampson, hunters, Brought into town, on their way to market, at San Francisco, a large quantity of ducks and other water fowl, as follows: fifty-eight teal, twenty-four curlew, seventeen spoon-bill, twenty-four willets, one broad-bill, one mallard, one canvass-back, and one gray duck. These were the results of a twenty-four hours’ hunt, and are exclusive of about three dozen of various kinds which were otherwise disposed of, making the whole number of birds killed, one hundred and fifty-one. This is but a fair sample of the number which two expert sportsmen might kill in twenty-four hours, to judge by the excellent facilities afforded, as told of by the hunters. While on this topic, it is but fair to speak of the hunting and fishing we ‘hear tell’ of in the mountains but a few miles off, and which we long to participate in, and hope to, in a short time. Quail are abundant almost beyond belief, and other small game are found in large quantities. Deer are numerous, and occasionally the hunter meets with an unwelcome prowler in the shape of a huge grizzly bear. A meeting with this latter-named animal was not included in the anticipated sport above spoken of.” T.GB.1860.18, Times Gazette, 4 February, 1860. descriptions.value: “A short time since two young men in passing through a thicket on the Merced, came suddenly upon an enormous : bear, who, without an instant's warning, sprung upon one of them, and with a blow of his paw struck his rifle from his hand, and dashed him to the ground. He then bit him severely in several places, rolling him over and over, lifting him at times on his nose, and tossing him into the bushes. Then clasping him in his fore paws, tearing his clothes and gnawing into his flesh, the bear would play with him as a cat would with a mouse,. Stunned by the first blow from the bear, the man was completely at his mercy, and made no attempt to defend himself or to escape. Having amused himself to his satisfaction, the bear left his victim, who gradually recovered and was enabled to crawl a short distance, towards his camp. He was found in a deplorable situation by some friends who had been informed of the occurrence by his companion, who supposed that bruin had made a meal of him. War was immediately declared against the monster, and after a severe fight which lasted some hours, he was killed.“ GB.1850.2, Daily Alta California, Volume 1, Number 45, 20 February 1850. descriptions.value: “One morning, while searching for acorns or ground nuts, they observed a herd of grizzly bears, intent upon making a similar morning meal. The sight of fresh animal food tempted the poor travellers to expend a portion of their scant ammunition in an endeavor to bring down one of these formidable beasts, and they discharged their pieces, without counting upon the result in the event of wounding one of them. One shot inflicted a mortal wound, while a wounded bruin and its full grown cub made directly at one of the men. Our informant had thrown down his rifle, and was in the act of climbing a sapling, when the bears turned from his comrade upon him. He was too weak to escape them, and the foremost dragged him to the earth. His hip joint was dislocated by the fall, and he was otherwise severely injured. He remained with his face downward, while the bears lacerated his flesh, and stripped his clothing from him, after which they left him, and he was found by his companions in a dreadful state of suffering. His wounds were dressed, and after a short time he was enabled to proceed slowly on the journey. The second day after, they reached the sea coast, at a point which they judged to be above the bay of Trinidad. They killed an eagle and devoured its flesh, and also sustained life by feeding on dead fish which were found upon the shore. Up to this time they had seen but a few Indians, but now they were visited by numbers who kindly supplied them with fish. After travelling some thirty miles along the coast, they found Trinity river — this they felt confident was no other stream, and they immediately retraced their steps coastwise, and in a couple of days they arrived at Trinidad Bay.“ , Daily Alta California, Volume 1, Number 86, 9 April 1850.
